title: Google Maps
brief: Design a maps app like Google Maps. Under one icon sit three different systems: a map you can pan and zoom, a router that finds the best path across a continent, and live traffic that changes how long that path takes. Each one is a different kind of problem.

functional: Show a map you can pan and zoom smoothly.
Search for a place or address and move the map there.
Find a route between two points and show the turns.
Show an estimated arrival time that reflects current traffic.
Collect anonymous location samples from moving devices to learn traffic.

nonFunctional.name: Map load
nonFunctional.target: Tiles for a screen appear in under 200 ms, mostly from a nearby cache

nonFunctional.name: Route latency
nonFunctional.target: A route anywhere on the continent in under 500 ms at the 99th percentile

nonFunctional.name: Traffic freshness
nonFunctional.target: Road speeds reflect what happened in the last few minutes

nonFunctional.name: Availability
nonFunctional.target: The base map works even when traffic or routing is down

nonFunctional.name: Privacy
nonFunctional.target: Traffic is aggregated, never shown or stored per person

api.does: Returns one tile. Served by the CDN, almost never reaching our servers.
Turns text into a ranked list of places with coordinates (geocoding).
Returns a path as a list of road segments, a distance and an ETA.
Turns a coordinate into the nearest address.
Uploads a batch of anonymous location samples with no user id.

data.why: Written offline, read by key. The key is the address, so caches work with no lookup.
A search must follow thousands of links in a millisecond. Disk or network hops would kill it.
Updated every few minutes for millions of segments. Old values just expire.

data.fields: placeId, name, address, lat, lng, category
data.store: Search index with a geo field.
data.why: Text matching, ranking and distance in one query. A plain key-value store cannot do that.

evolution.title: Draw each tile on request
evolution.problem: Start with the simplest thing that works: the app asks for the part of the map on screen, and a server draws it from the map data.
evolution.change: The API server reads roads and shapes, renders a picture and returns it. Fine for a demo, as every pan costs a render.

evolution.title: Pre-rendered tiles on a CDN
evolution.problem: Drawing is slow, and millions of people look at the same few places. Rendering each view again burns CPU for identical pictures.
evolution.change: Cut the world into a pyramid of tiles. Zoom 0 is one tile. Each level splits every tile into four, addressed by zoom, x and y. A builder renders them offline into a tile store, and a CDN serves them. The app works out which tiles cover the screen.
evolution.numbers: tiles at zoom z are 4 to the power z

evolution.title: The road network as a graph
evolution.problem: Tiles are pictures. They cannot answer 'how do I get from A to B?'.
evolution.change: Build a graph: junctions are nodes, road segments are edges with a length and travel time. A route service runs Dijkstra's algorithm over it, which grows a ring of nearest junctions until it reaches the goal. The graph is kept in memory.

evolution.title: Preprocess the graph
evolution.problem: Plain Dijkstra on a continent visits about half the junctions to cross it. That is minutes of CPU for one request, and we get thousands of requests per second.
evolution.change: Preprocess offline. Rank junctions by importance and add shortcut edges that skip minor stretches (contraction hierarchies). A query climbs from both ends, local road to highway to local road, and visits a few thousand junctions.
evolution.numbers: the estimator compares naive seconds with cores needed

evolution.title: Live traffic from probes
evolution.problem: Distance is not time. A road that is quick at 3 am is a jam at 5 pm, and the route and ETA must reflect it.
evolution.change: Phones send anonymous location samples. A queue feeds a streaming aggregator that snaps each sample to a road segment (map matching), groups by segment and minute, and writes an average speed to a fast store. Routing reads these speeds.

evolution.title: Place search and geocoding
evolution.problem: People type 'coffee near me' or an address, not coordinates. A route needs a start and end point first.
evolution.change: A place search service holds an index of names and addresses with locations. It matches text, ranks results by distance and relevance, and returns coordinates. The API passes those to the route service.

flows.name: Load the map for a screen

steps.say: The app knows the zoom level and the centre. It works out which tile addresses (z, x, y) cover the screen, usually a handful.
It asks the CDN for each tile by address. Most are cache hits from a server nearby.
On a miss the CDN fetches the tile from the tile store and keeps a copy for the next person.
The tile builder wrote that tile earlier, offline, from the map data. Updates are rebuilt in batches and get a new version.
The app sends the start and the destination coordinates to the API.
The API hands them to the route service.
The route service snaps both points to the nearest road segments, then searches the preprocessed graph using shortcuts.
It adds current travel time to each segment, using the live speeds. Meanwhile, phones keep sending anonymous samples to ingest.
The aggregator turns the samples into a speed for each segment per minute.
Fresh speeds are read by the route service when it computes travel time.
The user types an address. The app sends the text and the current map centre.
The API passes it to place search. Nearby matches are ranked higher.
It returns a list of places with coordinates. The app recentres the map and loads those tiles.

deepDives.title: Vector tiles or raster tiles
deepDives.question: What does a tile actually contain?

options.name: Raster (a picture)
options.pros: Trivial for the client: just draw an image. Looks identical everywhere.
options.cons: Large. Every style, language or label change needs a new set of pictures. Zoom between levels looks blurry.

options.name: Vector (shapes and labels)
options.pros: Small, and the client draws it. Smooth zoom, rotation, 3D and dark mode from the same data.
options.cons: The client needs a GPU renderer. Bad tiles are harder to debug.

deepDives.pick: Vector tiles, with raster as a fallback
deepDives.because: One tile set serves every style and language. The saving in bytes and the freedom to restyle outweigh the cost of rendering on the device. Satellite imagery stays raster.

deepDives.title: Fast routes at continental scale
deepDives.question: How do we answer a long route in well under a second?

options.name: Plain Dijkstra
options.cons: Visits about half the graph for a far destination. Too slow for continental trips.

options.name: A* with a straight-line guess
options.pros: Heads toward the goal and visits fewer junctions.
options.cons: Still searches a wide area, and the guess helps little on winding roads.

options.name: Preprocessing (hierarchies)
options.pros: Offline work adds shortcuts so a query visits thousands of junctions, not millions.
options.cons: Costly to rebuild, and the shortcuts bake in the edge weights.

deepDives.because: Roads rarely change but are queried constantly, so spend work once and save it on every query. Use A* or plain search only for short local routes.

deepDives.title: Fresh traffic on a static graph
deepDives.question: Shortcuts assume fixed travel times. Traffic changes them every minute.

options.name: Rebuild the whole hierarchy often
options.cons: Too slow and heavy to repeat every few minutes at continental scale.

options.name: Keep the shape, re-weight cheaply
options.pros: The graph structure and shortcuts stay. Only edge weights are recomputed, which is much faster.
options.cons: Queries are a little slower than a perfectly built hierarchy.

options.name: Historical speed profiles
options.pros: Typical speed for each segment by time of day and weekday. Needs no live data and is stable.

deepDives.pick: Re-weight on a fixed shape, blended with history
deepDives.because: Road layout changes weekly, but speeds change by the minute. Split the two. Use typical speeds as a baseline, nudge them with live data, and fall back to the baseline where samples are few.

deepDives.title: Turning probes into segment speeds
deepDives.question: How do we turn a stream of anonymous points into a speed per road?

options.name: Batch job every hour
options.pros: Simple. Plenty of data per segment.
options.cons: An hour old is useless for a jam that started 10 minutes ago.

options.name: Streaming windowed aggregation
options.pros: Group by segment and a one-minute window. Fresh, and the state is small.
options.cons: Handling late events and a bad map-match needs care. Sparse segments are noisy.

deepDives.pick: Streaming, with a minimum sample count
deepDives.because: Use a short window and publish a speed only if enough different devices contributed. This improves freshness, and the threshold also protects privacy, since no single person is visible. Drop the device id at ingest.

failures.what: A tile has stale or wrong content
failures.impact: Roads that closed are still drawn, or a new road is missing.
failures.fix: Version tiles. Rebuild changed areas first, and purge them from the CDN. Keep routing data on its own release path.

failures.impact: Speeds go stale, so ETAs drift and bad jams are missed.
failures.fix: Give every speed a timestamp and let it expire. Fall back to typical speeds by time of day. The map and routing keep working.

failures.what: Routing servers lose their in-memory graph
failures.impact: A restarted node cannot answer until it reloads gigabytes of graph.
failures.fix: Partition by region, run replicas, and load from a snapshot. Keep a node out of rotation until it is warm.

failures.what: A popular event floods one region's tiles
failures.impact: A burst of requests for the same few tiles misses cold caches.
failures.fix: Tile requests are cacheable, so most hits stay on the CDN. Use request collapsing so one miss fetches once, and pre-warm known event areas.

failures.impact: A sample is placed on the wrong road, such as a bridge instead of the highway below.
failures.fix: Match a short sequence of points, not one, using heading and road class. Reject low-confidence matches and require many samples.

scaling.limit: The road graph no longer fits on one server
scaling.lever: Partition by region with a small overlap, and route across regions through border nodes. Replicate each partition for load.

scaling.limit: Tile storage grows 4 times with each zoom level
scaling.lever: Build only tiles with content, use vector tiles, and render the deepest levels on demand and cache them.
Partition the stream by tile or region. Sample down on busy roads, since a hundred cars add little over twenty.
Rebuild per region and in parallel. Reuse the shape, and apply traffic changes only as new weights.

recap.key: Three systems in one app: pre-rendered tiles addressed by zoom, x and y on a CDN, a preprocessed road graph so routes are fast, and a streaming pipeline that turns anonymous probes into live segment speeds.
recap.numbers: About 69 billion tiles at zoom 18 (4 to the z). Plain Dijkstra on 500M junctions takes minutes, a preprocessed query visits thousands. 50M devices every 5 s is 10M samples per second.
moves: Cut the map into a zoom, x, y tile pyramid and serve it from a CDN
Model roads as a graph and preprocess it, because plain Dijkstra is too slow
Aggregate anonymous probes by segment and minute, then feed speeds to routing
Keep each system independent so a traffic outage cannot take down the map
